title: Manasseh's Evil and Manasseh's Repentance
summary: Manasseh undoes his father Hezekiah's reform, rebuilding high places, filling the temple courts with altars to the stars, burning his sons in the fire, practicing sorcery, and setting a carved image in God's house. When he ignores God's warnings, Assyrian commanders drag him to Babylon with a hook and shackles, and there he humbles himself and prays; God hears him and restores him to Jerusalem, where he removes the idols and restores the LORD's altar. His son Amon returns to the idols without repentance and is assassinated after two years.
story: Hezekiah was among the best of David's heirs; his son Manasseh begins as the worst. Chronicles lists his sins at length because they are the very abominations for which the Canaanites lost the land, and the temple that Hezekiah cleansed becomes a gallery of idols. Then the story does something unexpected. The worst king in Judah's history becomes the Bible's most striking example of repentance in its royal records. For the Chronicler's first readers, returned from exile in Babylon, the story had special force: if God heard Manasseh in Babylon and brought him home, he could hear them too. Amon's short reign follows as a contrast, a son who copied his father's sin but not his repentance. His death brings the boy Josiah to the throne.
historical:
Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, the longest of any king of Judah, in the first half of the seventh century BC; a common reconstruction places his reign at about 697 to 642 BC, possibly including a co-regency with Hezekiah. These were the decades of Assyria's greatest power, under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and Assyrian inscriptions from both kings list Manasseh of Judah among the western rulers who supplied tribute or building materials. Judah was a loyal vassal for most of this period.

2 Kings 21 tells of Manasseh's sins, adds that he shed much innocent blood, and names him as the reason the LORD would not turn from his anger against Judah (2 Kings 23:26; 24:3), but it says nothing of his captivity or repentance. Chronicles alone reports these. Some historians suggest the summons to Babylon may connect with Assyrian efforts to secure loyalty in the west during a Babylonian revolt against Ashurbanipal in the 650s BC, when Assyria controlled Babylon; others remain cautious because no Assyrian text mentions the event. Amon ruled about 642 to 640 BC. A later Jewish prayer attributed to Manasseh, the Prayer of Manasseh, is included in some Bibles among the Apocrypha, but most scholars date it much later than Manasseh, so it is not the text the Chronicler cites in verses 18-19 from sources now lost.
cultural:
The “host of heaven” (verse 3) refers to the sun, moon, and stars worshiped as deities, a practice widespread in Mesopotamia. Sorcery, divination, and consulting mediums were all forbidden by the Law (Deuteronomy 18:10-12) because they sought hidden knowledge and power apart from God. The carved image in the temple was probably an image of Asherah (2 Kings 21:7), the goddess whose poles appear throughout Kings and Chronicles.

The hook in the nose and bronze shackles (verse 11) were real practices; Assyrian reliefs show captives led by ropes attached to rings, and the image of a hook in the nose is used by the prophets for Assyria's own humiliation (Isaiah 37:29). Manasseh's building of the outer wall and stationing of commanders after his return fits a vassal restored to his post and trusted to guard a frontier. The note that the people still sacrificed at the high places, “but only to the LORD” (verse 17), shows that his reform stopped idolatry without fully centralizing worship at the temple.
literary: The chapter is built on reversal. Verses 1-9 catalog Manasseh's sins, deliberately set against God's promise about the temple and the land (verses 7-8). Verse 10 is the hinge: the LORD spoke, but they did not listen. Verses 11-13 tell the punishment and the prayer, and verses 14-17 reverse the earlier sins one by one: the idol removed, the altars dumped outside the city, the LORD's altar restored. Verse 13 contains one of the most moving lines in Chronicles: “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.” The Amon account (verses 21-25) is a short mirror, using the same verb of humbling to say that Amon “did not humble himself” (verse 23). The whole chapter illustrates God's words in 7:14 about a people who humble themselves, pray, and turn.

outline.t: Manasseh's idolatry and the corruption of the temple

doctrines.note: Manasseh's repentance comes in distress, after years of refusing to listen, yet God receives it. The chapter shows that no one is beyond the reach of repentance, and that genuine repentance produces concrete change.

God's response to Manasseh's prayer is grace, not wages. He restores a man who had filled his house with idols and killed his own sons. Chronicles presents this as the nature of God, not an exception.

Manasseh's sins show idolatry's full shape: false gods, occult practices, and child sacrifice, all brought into the place meant for God's Name. Idolatry corrupts not only worship but family and justice.

words.note: Kana, to be humbled or to humble oneself. It appears in verse 12 of Manasseh, in verse 19, and twice in verse 23 of Amon, who did not humble himself. It is God's own condition in 7:14 for hearing and healing, and Manasseh is its clearest example.

Atar, to plead or entreat. Used in verses 13 and 19, it describes earnest supplication, and it also describes God's willingness to be entreated. The same root is used when God responds to Isaac's prayer for Rebekah (Genesis 25:21).

Yada, to know. After his restoration, Manasseh knew that the LORD is God (verse 13). Knowing in Hebrew often means knowledge gained by experience, not merely information. Manasseh learned in captivity what he had refused to hear from the prophets.
Semel, image or statue. A rare word, used for the carved idol Manasseh set up in the temple (verses 7 and 15). Its removal in verse 15 is the clearest sign that his repentance was real.

christ: Manasseh's story is the Old Testament's great picture of mercy to the worst of sinners. The New Testament presents the same grace in Christ: Paul calls himself the foremost of sinners and says he received mercy so that Christ Jesus might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15-16). Jesus' parable of the lost son, who comes to his senses in a far country and returns to a father who runs to meet him (Luke 15:11-24), has often been read alongside Manasseh's return from Babylon. The link is thematic. Chronicles does not predict Christ here, but it shows the heart of the God whom Jesus revealed as the Father who receives sinners.

hard.q: Kings blames Manasseh for the exile and says nothing of his repentance. Why does Chronicles tell a different story?
hard.a: The two books tell the story for different purposes. Kings, completed during the exile, is explaining why Jerusalem fell, and it names Manasseh's sins as the tipping point (2 Kings 23:26; 24:3). Chronicles, written after the return, is showing its readers that repentance is always possible and that God hears those who humble themselves. Some scholars think the Chronicler used a reliable source unknown to the writer of Kings, pointing to the named records of the seers in verse 19. Others think the Chronicler has shaped Manasseh's long reign into a lesson about repentance, perhaps building on a real deportation. Both accounts can be true together: Manasseh's personal repentance did not undo the damage his decades of idolatry had done to the nation, as Amon's immediate relapse shows.

questions: Manasseh humbled himself only in distress, after years of refusing to listen. What does it take for you to hear God?
If God received Manasseh, who in your life (including yourself) have you considered beyond the reach of grace?
Manasseh's repentance did not reach his son Amon. How do our choices, both our sins and our repentance, shape the next generation?
